question.:question/problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂x}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂y}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=2r+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂x}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=2,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2r}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(r,\theta )={r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r}=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂g}{∂\theta }=-3{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-3{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =r(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta -3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )={r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂x}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=2r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(r,\theta)=- r^{2} (\cos {4 \theta} - 2)$, find $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$, where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂r}\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta}\sin \theta.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r}=- 2 r (\cos {4 \theta} - 2),\,\frac{∂f}{∂\theta}=4 r^{2} \sin {4 \theta}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(- 2 r (\cos {4 \theta} - 2))\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}(4 r^{2} \sin {4 \theta})\sin \theta \\ & =4r\cos \theta-2r\cos 4\theta\cos \theta-4r\sin 4\theta\sin \theta \\ & =-r(-4\cos \theta+2\cos 4\theta\cos \theta+4\sin 4\theta\sin \theta).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $u(r,\theta)=3 r^{3} (\cos {4 \theta} - 2)$, find $\frac{∂u}{∂x}$, where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$
\frac{∂u}{∂x}=\frac{∂u}{∂r}\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂u}{∂\theta}\sin \theta.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂r}=9 r^{2} (\cos {4 \theta} - 2),\,\frac{∂u}{∂\theta}=- 12 r^{3} \sin {4 \theta}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =(9 r^{2} (\cos {4 \theta} - 2))\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}(- 12 r^{3} \sin {4 \theta})\sin \theta \\ & =-18{r}^{2}\cos \theta+9{r}^{2}\cos 4\theta\cos \theta+12{r}^{2}\sin 4\theta\sin \theta \\ & =3{r}^{2}(-6\cos \theta+3\cos 4\theta\cos \theta+4\sin 4\theta\sin \theta).\end{aligned}
$$
